items.title: Elon Musk Plays Down G.O.P. Support After Midterm Loss
items.summary: The C.E.O. of SpaceX, who spent millions to back Republican candidates, sought to portray himself as a political moderate.
items.full_text:
Title: Elon Musk Plays Down G.O.P. Support After Midterm Loss - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/business/dealbook/elon-musk-midterms.html

Published Time: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:59:36 GMT

Markdown Content:
In the run-up to the midterm elections, Elon Musk deployed both his wealth — to the tune of [nearly $500 million](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/02/us/politics/elon-musk-midterm-spending.html) — and his public influence to help Republican candidates win.

But in the wake of Democrats’ resounding victory at the ballot box, Mr. Musk is seeking to portray himself as more of a political moderate, saying, “There are positives and negatives in both parties.”

“I’m not MAGA,” Mr. Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX and Tesla, said at the DealBook Summit on Wednesday. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

(Mr. Musk has previously declared himself MAGA — and even “[dark gothic MAGA](https://www.wsj.com/style/fashion/elon-musk-dark-maga-hat-cap-gothic-trump-81e963cf).”)

Mr. Musk’s remarks were his most extensive to date after his [midterms spending spree flopped.](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/06/us/politics/musk-trump-midterm-election-spending.html) He bluntly said his effort “failed, by the way, obviously.” And it had him questioning, at an existential level, whether spending money on politics even worked.

Mr. Musk spent more money on the election than any person ever has in a cycle where they themselves were not the candidate.

What about his spending millions in support of losing candidates [like Ken Paxton](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/16/us/politics/elon-musk-ken-paxton-texas-senate-race.html), who ran for the Senate in Texas? “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Mr. Musk conceded. “Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”

The pivot by Mr. Musk was the latest effort by business leaders to [grapple with the aftermath of the midterms](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/technology/tech-billionaires-democrats-midterms.html), particularly as newly empowered Democrats took aim at billionaires and businesses like data centers.

Throughout the interview, Mr. Musk largely avoided the often fiery (and [sometimes profane](https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/29/business/dealbook/elon-musk-advertisers-blackmail-iger.html)) declarations that punctuated his last appearance at the DealBook Summit, in 2023. He predicted that things in Texas would be “fine” under Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor, who supports maintaining a moratorium on new data centers in the state. Mr. Musk, a Texas resident, called her “quite moderate” and “not a far-left governor.”

Mr. Musk spoke at length about less politically divisive topics, like potentially merging SpaceX and Tesla and helping humanity achieve interstellar travel.

He also defended Jensen Huang, the former chief executive of the chip maker Nvidia, whom he described as “a friend of mine” and whom he supported returning to that role. Though American intelligence considers that an executive whom Mr. Huang had an affair with was a Chinese intelligence asset, Mr. Musk said, “I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States.”

Still, Mr. Musk was willing to be combative, particularly when it came to Ukraine.

Addressing restrictions on the Ukrainian military’s access to the satellite communications network that SpaceX runs, Mr. Musk said that the system, Starlink, was never meant to be used for offensive strikes in war.

“Do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions that sometimes result in the loss of innocent lives,” Mr. Musk said.

When asked about claims by Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, that his country’s forces were using the military version of Starlink — which can be used for attacks — Mr. Musk shot back, “He’s not always truthful.”

items.title: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military
items.summary: Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant behind the company at the center of the Nvidia spy saga, has used its A.I. computing technology to aid a lab with links to China’s military.
items.full_text:
Title: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/nvidia-alibaba-china-military.html

Published Time: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:47:19 GMT

Markdown Content:
In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.

Working from a colonial mansion in the city’s former French Concession neighborhood, the couple boasted about Ms. Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, who they said would guarantee a supply of powerful computer chips.

They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.

Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.

For the past several weeks, [Nvidia has been convulsed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/nvidia-jensen-huang-affair-colette-kress.html) by revelations that Mr. Huang had an [extramarital relationship](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen-huang-nvidia-board.html) with [Alice Huang](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/technology/alice-huang-megaspeed-nvidia-jensen-huang.html?searchResultPosition=4), whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.

The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.

The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.

Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.

The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.

In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.

In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. [Mr. Huang resigned](https://www.nytimes.com/video/business/economy/100000011279681/nvidia-jensen-huang-ceo-resigns-affairs.html?searchResultPosition=9) last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.

Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military [issued hundreds](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/01/business/economy/china-military-nvidia-chips.html) of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

“Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.

James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.

Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.

“Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”

Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.

Image

![Image 1: A glass door opens to a lobby with the sign Megaspeed.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/16/multimedia/00-Alibaba-Spy-2-03-wtml/00-Alibaba-Spy-2-03-wtml-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Megaspeed quickly became a major buyer of Nvidia’s powerful A.I. chips.Credit...The New York Times

## ‘An incredible hero’

During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.

Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.

“He is the hero. He’s an incredible hero. A superhero,” Mr. Huang said to Mr. Wang onstage, noting his work with young people. It is not clear if he knew of the lab’s military ties.

Image

Jensen Huang, right, the former Nvidia chief executive, with Wang Jian, the founder of Alibaba Cloud and leader of Zhejiang Lab, in 2025 in Beijing.Credit...Zhao Wenyu/China News Service, via VCG, via Getty Images

Mr. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Wang stretched back more than a decade. After Mr. Wang built Alibaba’s cloud unit, it became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying chips for a cloud service that was used by businesses and government.

The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.

But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.

Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.

At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.

A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.

Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.

A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.

Image

Zhejiang Lab in Hangzhou

items.title: What to Do Before the Next Big Tech Outage?
items.summary: A cascade of recent tech failures has rattled Americans and prompted many to look for ways to prepare for a prolonged digital disruption. Experts say it’s much like preparing for a storm.
items.full_text:
Title: What to Do Before the Next Big Tech Outage? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/technology/tech-outages-emergency-prep.html

Published Time: Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:48:15 GMT

Markdown Content:
After a series of unsettling tech failures rattled airline passengers and other consumers in recent days, people may be wondering if there is anything they can do to prepare for the next outage.

Of the most recent disruptions, the longest — [a global outage of Microsoft’s services](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/microsoft-outage-what-to-know.html) — was resolved on Saturday after about 36 hours. A [rare national ground stop](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html) that stranded thousands of airline passengers on Friday was lifted after more than four hours, but its aftershocks lingered. On Monday, some [Chase Bank customers](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/16/us/bank-outages-down.html) were briefly unable to use their A.T.M. cards or complete transactions.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said [on Wednesday](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/world/asia/tech-outages-cyberattack-hack-rubio.html) that there was “zero” evidence that the failures were related or that they were the work of a foreign power or hackers.

But whatever the cause, what if the next one tests our dependence on digital services like phone-based payment systems or online banking? And what if it persists for days?

Here are some steps people can take to prepare.

## Keep cash on hand.

Image

It’s smart to have small bills at home, along with bank account numbers written or printed on paper, said Chris Krebs, a cybersecurity expert.Credit...Anna Watts for The New York Times

One habit people should embrace again is having a little cash on hand, said Chris Krebs, a former director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

Mr. Krebs, who now runs the Krebs Group, a cybersecurity and geopolitical risk management consultancy, said he was “as guilty as anybody of not having any cash” around. But he said it was good to have small bills at home, along with bank account numbers written or printed on paper.

“Folks need to be thinking: Hey, the last couple of days with all these disruptions, these were the things I wasn’t able to do because of a short-term disruption,” he said. “How do I build personal resilience around that? What’s the thing that, if that fails, even if it’s just an hour or two, is there anything I can personally do?”

## How many phone numbers have you memorized?

The federal government’s disaster preparedness initiative, Ready.gov, [has a guide](https://www.ready.gov/sites/default/files/2020-03/family-emergency-communication-planning-document.pdf) for creating an emergency communication plan with your family. The first tip is to create a paper copy of contact information for relatives and close friends, as well as a list of other important numbers, such as for schools and doctors.

If this guidance sounds familiar, that’s because it is in line with what disaster preparedness experts advise for other kinds of disruptions, including power outages and wildfires.

Why so similar? Because, Mr. Krebs said, in a natural disaster, services that people depend on, such as water, electricity and gas, may go down and may take time to restore. “It’s not that much different to expect that, as everything is becoming digitized, that some of those digital services could have temporary outages,” he said.

“Everybody’s feeling this personally because every aspect of our lives is riding on some digital dependency, whether it’s checking the bank, talking to your loved ones, figuring out schedules for your kids on the weekend, whatever,” Mr. Krebs said. “And so when there’s a disruption to any of those services, you feel it, you feel it immediately, and you realize that you don’t have a fallback plan. There’s no analog version anymore of your iPhone.”

## Prepare for an outage as you would a storm.

Image

The federal government’s disaster preparedness initiative, Ready.gov, suggests creating a paper copy of important phone numbers.Credit...Justin Sullivan/Getty Images

It’s smart to have a three-day preparedness plan, just like the one people should have in case of a physical emergency.

Chetrice Romero, a senior cybersecurity adviser at the law firm Ice Miller, suggested that people keep one gallon of water per day for each member of their household and three days of nonperishable food, charged power banks and flashlights.

The federal government has a number of [resources](https://www.ready.gov/be-informed) for creating plans for a range of emergencies, including avalanches, cyberattacks and wildfires, including [no-cost or low-cost preparation tips](https://www.ready.gov/low-and-no-cost) and tips specific to certain populations, such as [caregivers](https://www.ready.gov/caregivers).

One difference with tech outages is that they happen suddenly, whereas bad weather is often preceded by hours or even days of warnings, Ms. Romero noted.

“These outages, I think, create a lot more anxiety because you think you’re fine and then you’re not,” she said. “And then it’s hard to explain what’s wrong, right? We know bad weather is bad weather. It’s hard for people to wrap their heads around ones and zeros they don’t understand.”

She said she hoped the recent outages would get people thinking about being prepared for tech outages as they would for a storm.

## Be alert for scams.

When technological failures happen, Ms. Romero said, one immediate concern is that bad actors will prey on the anxieties in order to scam people.

If you receive an email or text claiming to be from your bank or a company whose services you use and it asks for private information, like a Social Security or account number, do not respond, she said. “Go straight to your bank, communicate directly with them,” she said, adding, “verify, verify, verify.”

Also, voices can be imitated, so if a loved one calls and claims they need money to be transferred to them immediately because their bank is down, hang up and call them at a number you know is theirs.
